job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Drafting Problems in S. 2817 (Manager's Amendment of Oct. 6, 2026)

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-metric-ton cap applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could split production across several vessels, each staying under the limit. Nothing aggregates tonnage by operator, project, or license area.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), undefined measurement terms.** "Per year" (calendar, fiscal, or rolling 12 months), the tonnage basis (wet or dry), and "recovery" (collection on the seabed or lifting to the surface) are all undefined. These gaps invite disputes over whether the threshold was crossed.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), depth and "seabed" ambiguity.** The text doesn't say whether "depths greater than 200 meters" means water depth or depth below the seabed surface. It also doesn't say whether "from the seabed" covers subsurface deposits, such as sulfides or crusts that require cutting or drilling.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" may be overbroad.** In other federal statutes, such as the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, "minerals" includes oil and gas. Read that way, the definition could sweep in offshore hydrocarbon production or sand and gravel recovery. That creates both an overbreadth challenge and new opponents.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary" is undefined.** The Act never says which Secretary (Commerce, Interior, or State) holds this authority. The provision may be unworkable until that is clarified.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), delegated definition of a crime.** The agency would effectively define what conduct is criminal (Sec. 5(b)), using a vague "comparable risks" standard with no criteria and no required procedure. This invites nondelegation, void-for-vagueness, and due process challenges. After *Loper Bright*, the agency's determinations would also get no judicial deference.

7. **Sec. 2(2), narrow "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and "corporation[s] organized under the laws of a State." It omits:
   - LLCs, partnerships, and trusts
   - entities organized in D.C. or the territories (unless "State" is defined elsewhere)
   - lawful permanent residents
   - foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies

   A U.S. company could restructure or operate abroad through a foreign affiliate, including one sponsored through the ISA.

8. **Sec. 2(3), covered vessel threshold.** The registry applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons. Smaller vessels, or vessels not permanently "equipped for" recovery (for example, with modular or leased equipment), fall outside it entirely.

9. **Secs. 2(1)(A) and 2(3), terminology mismatch.** The prohibition counts tonnage by "a single vessel" (any vessel), while the registry uses "covered vessel." Production from unregistered small vessels could escape both monitoring and the threshold calculation.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

10. **Sec. 3(a), activities not reached.** The bill bars only "engag[ing] in" mining. It does not address financing, sponsoring, chartering vessels to, conspiring with, or aiding foreign miners, nor importing, purchasing, or processing nodules mined abroad. U.S. firms could support or buy from foreign operations without restriction.

11. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States" undefined.** The text doesn't say whether "United States" includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the continental shelf. It also doesn't say whether a foreign firm directing offshore operations from a U.S. office is a "person in the United States."

12. **Sec. 3(b), the grandfather clause may swallow the rule.** It exempts "mining conducted under an exploration license" issued before enactment, with no limit on duration, renewal, transfer, amendment, or expansion. Arguably it also permits commercial-scale mining by any existing licensee.

13. **Sec. 3(b), license vs. permit confusion.** The Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA) distinguishes exploration *licenses* from commercial recovery *permits*. The bill doesn't say whether "mining under an exploration license" means exploration only. It also doesn't say whose licenses count: NOAA, the ISA, or foreign sponsoring states.

14. **Sec. 3(b), date mismatch creates a rush window.** Licenses issued before enactment are grandfathered, so applicants have an incentive to secure licenses before the bill is signed. Meanwhile, the prohibition itself doesn't take effect until 180 days later (Sec. 8).

15. **Sec. 3(c), open-ended "environmental assessment" exception.** The exception turns on subjective "purpose" and has none of the following:
   - a definition
   - a tonnage cap
   - a permit or approval requirement
   - agency oversight
   - a bar on selling recovered material

   Pilot or full-scale mining could be labeled as assessment.

## Sec. 4: Registry

16. **Sec. 4, no penalty for noncompliance.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report, or filing false reports, carries no penalty under this Act. A prosecution for false statements under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 might still be possible.

17. **Sec. 4, no deadlines, content, or verification.** There is no registration deadline and "operator" is undefined. The reports need not state tonnage, depth, or location, and they are self-certified, with no inspection, observer, vessel-tracking, or audit authority. As a result, the reports cannot reliably show whether the 10,000-ton threshold was exceeded.

18. **Sec. 4, unclear reach over foreign-flag vessels.** The text doesn't say whether foreign-flagged vessels operated by foreign operators must register. If they must, jurisdictional and international law objections are likely.

19. **Sec. 4, no rulemaking or implementing authority.** NOAA is given no authority to issue regulations, forms, or procedures. The agency named here (NOAA) may also differ from "the Secretary" in Sec. 2(1)(B).

## Sec. 5: Penalties

20. **Sec. 5(a), effective-date conflict.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days after enactment (Sec. 8). This creates confusion and a potential fair-notice or retroactivity argument for conduct during that window.

21. **Sec. 5(a), per-day penalty vs. annual threshold.** Violation is defined by annual tonnage, but penalties accrue "for each day." It is unclear when a violation begins: on the day the cumulative tonnage passes 10,000, or retroactively for the whole year.

22. **Sec. 5, no enforcement machinery.** The section names no enforcing agency, no administrative or judicial assessment process, and no jurisdiction or venue provision. It also grants no subpoena, boarding, inspection, seizure, or forfeiture authority. Enforcement against at-sea operations would be very difficult.

23. **Sec. 5(b), criminal liability tied to vague definitions.** Ten-year felony exposure attached to an agency-defined offense (Sec. 2(1)(B)) and to ambiguous terms like "recovery" and "environmental assessment" strengthens vagueness and rule-of-lenity defenses.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

24. **Sec. 6, hortatory and ambiguous deadline.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" doesn't say whether negotiations must *begin* or *conclude* within 18 months, and there is no consequence for failure. Directing the Executive's negotiating posture may also draw separation-of-powers objections, and the U.S. is not a party to UNCLOS or a member of the ISA.

## Sec. 7: Duration

25. **Sec. 7(a), no trigger for the report.** NASEM is never directed or funded to produce the report, and there is no timeline. "Serious harm" is undefined.

26. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), internal conflict.** Subsection (a) says the ban lasts until Congress makes a finding, while (b) ends the whole Act at 10 years regardless. Which provision controls is unclear.

27. **Sec. 7(b), sunset has no savings clause.** The sunset terminates the entire Act, including penalties, and the sunset date runs from enactment rather than from the effective date. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) addresses repeals, and whether it covers expirations is unsettled, so pending enforcement actions could arguably lapse.

## Sec. 8 and Structural Gaps

28. **Sec. 8, 180-day window.** The delay lets operators ramp up activity, restructure entities, reflag vessels, or move operations offshore before the prohibition bites.

29. **Whole Act, no relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or reconcile DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.), OCSLA, or existing NOAA licenses and permits. That leaves conflicting statutory regimes and arguments that the earlier, more specific statutes still authorize activity.

30. **Whole Act, no severability clause.** If a provision such as Sec. 2(1)(B) is struck down, there is no express direction on whether the rest survives.

31. **Whole Act, possible takings claims.** Holders of DSHMRA rights or pending applications not covered by Sec. 3(b) may bring Fifth Amendment takings or reliance-based claims.

32. **Whole Act, missing definitions.** Several key terms are undefined: "Secretary," "person," "United States," "seabed," "recovery," "polymetallic nodules," "operator," "exploration license," and "environmental assessment."

**Note for markup prep:** Items 5, 16, 20, 26, and 30 are simple drafting fixes that the sponsors or committee staff could easily correct by amendment. Expect them to be cleaned up if raised. The more substantive issues (items 1, 6, 7, 10, 12, 15, and 29) are harder to fix without changing the bill's scope, and they are likely to remain live points of debate.
